Stretch, Not Strain

Faculty professional development · 45 to 60 minutes (30-minute version below) · Led by counseling and learning support · Middle and Upper School, any subject

Session plan

A suggested plan. Change the timing, skip or reorder slides, or use any part on its own. You know your students.

Goal

Teachers leave knowing what the research says about productive struggle, able to tell a student who is stretching from one who is shutting down, and with two or three classroom moves to try the next week.

Materials

  • Index cards, a few per person
  • Teachers bring one upcoming unit or problem set of their own
  • The faculty quick reference (last slide): one page to print or keep open

Flow

  1. 5 minOpening: a student who shut down (private cards)
  2. 5 minThe question the department asked
  3. 12 minThe research on the right amount of struggle (4 studies)
  4. 8 minStretch or shutdown, and why students opt out
  5. 8 minThe research on getting them back in (3 studies)
  6. 5 minFive moves for Monday
  7. 8 minThree students (small groups)
  8. 4 minOne move this week

Short on time (20-minute advisory)

Thirty minutes: the question (3), the 80% finding and worked examples (6), stretch or shutdown (5), wise feedback and reappraisal (6), five moves (5), one move this week (5). Share the faculty quick reference afterward.

Before you present
Two presenters, one voice.

A natural split: the counselor or psychologist presents the stress and motivation research (the shutdown loop, reappraisal, wise feedback, mindset), and learning support presents the instructional research (desirable difficulties, the 80% finding, worked examples, productive failure). Each of you can take one of the student scenarios in the debrief.

Nobody here is doing it wrong.

Teachers asked for this because they care. Keep it practical and avoid any hint that student struggle is the teacher's fault. Most people in the room have watched a student shut down and felt stuck too.

Name the teacher's discomfort.

Watching a student struggle is hard, and rescuing is a kind instinct. Part of this talk is helping adults sit with a student's discomfort a little longer, the same skill we're asking of students.

Shutdown and crisis are different.

This talk is about everyday academic struggle. A student who seems hopeless, panicked most days, or unsafe needs a counselor the same day. Teachers don't screen or diagnose; they notice and walk the student over.

Be honest about the evidence.

Several studies used college students or adults, and some effects are modest. Teachers trust a presenter who says so. Where a move comes from classroom practice rather than a study (the hint ladder, time-boxing), say that too.

Learning plans are scaffolds.

Extended time, notes, or a quiet space under a learning plan keep a student in the stretch zone. Frame them that way, never as a shortcut. Middle School students usually need the moves more visible (a printed hint ladder, a timer on the board).

Every student in the room

Culture, family, identity, ability and money: what to keep in mind for this topic.

Language learners.

A student learning English may be stuck on the words, not the science. Glossaries, sentence starters, and worked examples in plain language lower the language load so the real challenge is the content.

Learning differences and ADHD.

Working memory limits mean some students need worked examples longer and fade more slowly. That's a pacing choice, not a lower bar.

Students who expect to be judged.

Students from groups stereotyped as weaker in a subject (for example girls in physics, or Black and Latino students in advanced classes) may read struggle as proof the stereotype is right. Wise feedback was tested with exactly these students.

Who has help at home.

Some students go home to a parent who can explain chemistry or pay a tutor. Others go home to younger siblings to watch. Scaffolds that live in class (hint cards, worked examples) even that out.

Asking for help varies.

In some families and cultures, asking a teacher a question can feel disrespectful, or admitting confusion feels shameful. Make help-seeking a normal, built-in step rather than a personal risk.

Faith, fasting, and home stress.

A student who is fasting, grieving, or dealing with something at home has less to give that day. A dip in effort is worth a quiet check-in before it's treated as attitude.

What the research says

Learning conditions that make practice harder in the short term, like spacing, mixing problem types, and testing yourself, often produce better long-term learning. How well students perform during practice is a poor guide to how much they're learning.

Bjork & Bjork, 2011, Psychology and the Real World

Vygotsky described the zone of proximal development: the gap between what a learner can do alone and what they can do with guidance. Teaching aimed there moves development forward.

Vygotsky, 1978, Mind in Society

Rosenshine's review of research on effective teachers found the most successful teachers kept students at a high success rate during practice, around 80%.

Rosenshine, 2012, American Educator

Algebra students who studied worked examples learned faster and solved similar problems better than students who solved the same problems on their own.

Sweller & Cooper, 1985, Cognition and Instruction

Gradually removing steps from worked examples (fading) helps students move from studying examples to solving problems on their own.

Renkl & Atkinson, 2003, Educational Psychologist

Students who first tried to solve a new kind of problem, then got instruction, often showed deeper understanding and transfer than students taught first. It works when the struggle is designed and followed by teaching that builds on the students' attempts.

Kapur, 2016, Educational Psychologist

Students told that a racing heart before a test is the body preparing to perform scored higher on GRE math practice and on the real exam months later.

Jamieson et al., 2010, Journal of Experimental Social Psychology

Critical feedback paired with a note about high standards and the teacher's belief that the student could meet them made 7th graders more likely to revise their essays, with the largest effect for Black students who had lower trust in school.

Yeager et al., 2014, Journal of Experimental Psychology: General

Across two meta-analyses, growth-mindset interventions on their own had small average effects on achievement, with larger effects for students at risk or from lower-income families.

Sisk et al., 2018, Psychological Science
